channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of May 14-20, 1984 — Telenet Locks the Dial-Up Door
item.description: A new device promises to bar unauthorized callers from computer systems reached over telephone lines. WASHINGTON — GTE Telenet introduced a device Tuesday, May 15, designed to lock unauthorized users out of computer systems reached through telephone lines. The announcement turns the fast-growing worry over modem intrusion into a commercial hardware market. Also this week: Atari Pledges a Sober XL Comeback · Lucasfilm Turns Its Cameras Toward Games · Sub-$100 Modems Call the Home Office.

item.title: Week of May 7-13, 1984 — Lucasfilm Brings the Force to Home Videogames
item.description: The film studio unveils Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus!, two Atari projects built around fresh technology and a cinematic sense of play. SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — Lucasfilm publicly entered the home videogame market May 8, unveiling the first two projects from a Games Group nurtured through its collaboration with Atari. The announcement puts one of cinema's most famous technical workshops behind software intended for Atari 8-bit computers and the 5200 console. Also this week: Pens and Tablets Challenge the Keyboard · Home Word Processing Drops Below $100 · Atari Searches for a New Mission.

item.title: Week of April 30-May 6, 1984 — Hanover's 650,000 Visitors See the Portable Future
item.description: Epson lifts the lid on a lap-size LCD machine as Commodore signals a 16-bit business turn. HANOVER, West Germany — One of Europe's largest computer fairs drew roughly 650,000 visitors this week, turning the exhibition floor into a vivid measure of how quickly electronic computing is moving from specialist rooms toward desks, briefcases and homes. Also this week: Chuck Peddle Rides Back to Victor with the PlusPC · One Box, Two Computer Worlds · Can a Computer Teach Music? · Early Macintosh Verdict: Brilliant, but Boxed In.

item.title: Week of April 23-29, 1984 — Apple Puts the II in a Carrying Case
item.description: The $1,295 Apple IIc brings 128K, a built-in disk drive and nearly a decade of Apple II software into a compact 7.5-pound package. SAN FRANCISCO — Apple Computer unveiled the Apple IIc on April 24 at its “Apple II Forever” dealer convention, putting the durable Apple II design into an ivory case small enough to carry by its handle. Even a 6.2-magnitude earthquake shaking Moscone Center could not upstage the week’s landmark personal-computer announcement. Also this week: Apple II Forever, Apple III No More · IBM’s PCjr Stumbles Out of the Gate · Software Becomes the Machine’s Magic · April’s Game Shelf Spans Machines.

item.title: Week of April 16-22, 1984 — Software Steps Into the Spotlight
item.description: TIME puts the programs inside the machine on its April 16 cover as applications, compatibility and ease of use begin deciding the personal-computer contest. The personal-computer business has spent years selling the wonder of the machine itself. This week, the spotlight swings decisively to the programs that make those machines useful. TIME’s April 16 cover story, “The Wizard Inside the Machine,” calls software the magic carpet to the future and captures an industry learning that specifications alone do not close the sale. Also this week: Macintosh Meets the User-Group Crowd · Atari Sends Arcade Names to Rival Machines · PCjr and Macintosh Court the Newcomer.

item.title: Week of April 9-15, 1984 — HomeWord Brings Icons to Three Computer Camps
item.description: Sierra On-Line gives Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari owners the same $49.95 picture-guided word processor. A filing cabinet, a printed page, a printer, a disorderly page with an arrow, a question mark and a floppy disk now stand between the home writer and the command line. Sierra On-Line has introduced HomeWord for the Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari families, using six pictured icons to guide the program's principal jobs. Also this week: Atari's Games Defect to the Competition · War Games Grow Up on the Commodore 64 · The $100 Home Computer Is No Longer a Fantasy · Color Graphics Become a $39.95 C64 Tool.

item.title: Week of April 2-8, 1984 — The Peanut Meets the Mac: IBM and Apple Fight for the Next Home Buyer
item.description: TIME's April 2 report frames two incompatible visions of personal computing, one betting on compatibility, the other on the mouse. The comparison that dealers have been making informally since January reached the national press this week. In its April 2 technology report, TIME set IBM's PCjr against Apple's Macintosh and described the two as new entries battling for attention from the same undecided buyer. The deck put it plainly: new entries from IBM and Apple battle for attention. Also this week: Atari Invades Rival Machines With a Dozen Atarisoft Games · PC Boom Turns Into a Stock-Market Crapshoot · Mindset Pushes PC Graphics Beyond the IBM Mold · Jobs Sells the Macintosh as a Mission, Not Just a Machine.

item.title: Week of March 26-April 1, 1984 — AT&T Throws Down a Unix Gauntlet With Six 3B Computers
item.description: The post-divestiture giant puts Unix System V and its own 32-bit architecture at the center of a sweeping commercial challenge. AT&T formally entered the general-purpose computer business on March 27, opening a campaign that reaches from a desktop multi-user machine to fault-tolerant systems. Only months after the Bell System divestiture, the company is carrying Bell Labs software and AT&T-designed processors into direct competition with IBM, DEC, Data General, Wang and Hewlett-Packard. Also this week: Police Raids Put Britain’s Games-Cassette Pirates Under Pressure · IBM Rations PCs and XTs as the Component Squeeze Bites · Sinclair Microdrives Reach London Shops · Macintosh Commands the West Coast Computer Faire.

item.title: Week of March 19-25, 1984 — Mindset PC Bets on Custom Color Graphics
item.description: An 80186, MS-DOS and purpose-built video hardware aim the new machine at artists, animators and game makers. The newest challenge to the IBM-shaped personal-computer market arrives with a very different sales pitch: do more with the picture. InfoWorld placed the Mindset computer on its March 19 cover under the teasing line “Gambling on Great Graphics,” giving the ambitious machine one of the week’s most conspicuous introductions. Also this week: Microcomputers Become Tools of Independence · Laserdiscs Point Toward an Arcade-Style Future at Home · Chequered Flag Takes the British Micro Pole.

item.title: Week of March 12-18, 1984 — Timex Pulls the Plug on Its Sinclair Home Computers
item.description: The watchmaker joins Texas Instruments and Mattel in retreat, turning the post-boom home-computer shakeout into the week’s unmistakable story. Timex will cease production and sales of its Timex/Sinclair 1500 and 2068 home computers, ending one of the most visible attempts to put a microcomputer into American homes at a mass-market price. The company says manufacturing will stop after remaining components are used, probably within four months. Also this week: Mindset Bets Its PC Future on Spectacular Graphics · VisiCalc Partners Carry Their Feud to Softcon · Model 100 Gains a Desktop-Sized Disk Drive.

item.title: Week of March 5-11, 1984 — Software Steps Out of Hardware’s Shadow
item.description: A multibillion-dollar American trade looks overseas—and a software show makes clear that programs now constitute an industry of their own. The personal-computer business has spent years measuring progress in processors, memory and disk drives. This week the programs themselves claim the marquee. A March 4 report in The Washington Post describes American personal-computer software as a multibillion-dollar business whose firms are looking beyond the domestic boom toward customers overseas. Also this week: IBM’s PCjr Arrives to a Skeptical Reception · Micro Games Crowd the Chart · Industry Seeks Laws Against “Electronic Trespassers”.

item.title: Week of February 27-March 4, 1984 — IBM Packs the PC Into a 30-Pound Portable
item.description: Big Blue answers the transportable-computer boom with a suitcase-sized machine that runs familiar PC software. IBM announced the Portable Personal Computer 5155 Model 68 on February 29, bringing its own badge to a transportable category pioneered by Osborne and sharpened by Compaq. The new machine preserves IBM PC disk and software compatibility in a luggable case intended to move between desks. Also this week: West Coast Computer Faire Throws Open Its Doors · Software Becomes the Industry’s Main Event · PCjr Brings Better Games—and Awkward Compromises.

item.title: Week of February 20-26, 1984 — Zenith Joins the IBM-Compatible Rush With New 16-Bit PCs
item.description: The electronics veteran enters the hottest race in personal computing with a 16-bit family built to speak IBM’s language. Zenith Data Systems unveiled its Z-150 family on February 22, placing another substantial manufacturer in the fast-growing market for machines compatible with the IBM Personal Computer. The new 16-bit line is aimed at buyers who want access to the expanding IBM software world without buying an IBM-badged machine. Also this week: IBM and Eagle Settle Firmware Copyright Fight · Software Industry Comes Into Its Own · PC Magazine Pits Apple Experience Against IBM Momentum.

item.title: Week of February 13-19, 1984 — IBM Packs the PC into a 30-Pound Suitcase
item.description: The $4,225 Portable Personal Computer answers Compaq with PC/XT compatibility, twin floppy drives and a built-in amber screen. IBM entered the suitcase-computer contest on February 16 with the Portable Personal Computer model 5155, putting the familiar IBM PC architecture into a transportable case. Contemporary coverage made the competitive target plain: Compaq had proved that business buyers wanted a machine they could carry between offices without leaving their software behind. Also this week: Sinclair Sets a $499 American Course for the QL · CBS, IBM and Sears Bet on a Videotex Home · Coleco Courts Publishers for Adam “Best Of” Albums.

item.title: Week of February 6-12, 1984 — IBM Compatibility Becomes the Industry’s New Battleground
item.description: An open hardware architecture, protected firmware and a vast software library turn “compatible” into the most valuable—and confusing—word in personal computing. The flood of machines claiming kinship with the IBM Personal Computer has made compatibility one of the microcomputer trade’s most important and confusing questions. IBM published enough of the PC’s hardware design to invite expansion cards and outside development, but the machine’s basic input-output system remains copyrighted software. A look-alike case and an 8088-family processor alone do not make a true substitute. Also this week: Coleco Restarts Adam Lines After a Gentleman’s C · “Best Of” Game Albums Promised for Adam · One Printer Attempts Double Duty.

item.title: Week of January 30-February 5, 1984 — Macintosh Meets the Public in Boston
item.description: Steve Jobs brings Apple’s new graphical computer before the Boston Computer Society for its first public demonstration. BOSTON, Jan. 30 — Six days after Apple formally introduced Macintosh, Steve Jobs carried the compact computer onto the Boston Computer Society stage for what the society’s founder remembers as its first public showing. Before a room of experienced personal-computer users, the machine’s windows, icons and mouse moved from advertising promise to a working demonstration. Also this week: IBM Takes the Clone War to Court · Lisa 2 Becomes Macintosh’s Elder Sibling · MacWrite and MacPaint Make the Desktop Tangible · Computer Games Ask What Comes After the Crash.

item.title: Week of January 23-29, 1984 — Macintosh Arrives: Apple Bets $2,495 on the Mouse
item.description: The compact 128K machine brings Lisa-style windows, icons and graphics to a far wider market—and seeks a place beside the Apple II and IBM PC. CUPERTINO, Calif.—Apple Computer unveiled the Macintosh on January 24, placing a mouse-controlled graphical desktop inside a compact 20-pound machine carrying a suggested retail price of $2,495. Apple chairman Steven P. Jobs declared that the company expected Macintosh to become a third industry standard alongside the Apple II and IBM PC. Also this week: Lisa 2 Family Cuts the Price of Apple’s Workstation · MacWrite and MacPaint Lead the Software Parade · Atari Reorders the Front Office as the Game Crash Bites · Satellite Television Aims Straight at the Home.

item.title: Week of January 16-22, 1984 — APPLE'S ‘1984’ SPOT PUTS MACINTOSH ON THE NATIONAL STAGE
item.description: A stark Super Bowl film promises a new kind of personal computer before viewers have even seen the machine itself. During Super Bowl XVIII on January 22, Apple Computer used a single dramatic national broadcast to introduce the Macintosh as more than another machine. Ridley Scott’s film showed gray ranks of workers facing a giant screen until a lone runner smashed it, closing with Apple’s promise that 1984 would not resemble George Orwell’s 1984. Also this week: APPLE READIES A 32-BIT FAMILY AROUND MACINTOSH AND LISA 2 · COMMODORE 264 BETS ON SOFTWARE BUILT INTO THE MACHINE · COLECO PROMISES A LARGER ADAM WORLD AMID QUALITY QUESTIONS.

item.title: Week of January 9-15, 1984 — TRAMIEL QUITS COMMODORE
item.description: Founder’s surprise Friday resignation, days after his CES appearance, leaves the company’s next generation under a cloud. Jack Tramiel resigned as president and chief executive of Commodore International on Friday, January 13, an abrupt break at the company he had driven from office-machine roots into the center of the home-computer boom. The news followed only days after Tramiel personally championed Commodore’s new 264 family at the Winter Consumer Electronics Show. Also this week: Games Trade Finds Guarded Relief at CES · Commodore’s 264 Family Promises an Office in ROM · Coleco Builds an Adam Comeback Plan.

item.title: Week of January 2-8, 1984 — Commodore's 264 family steals a shakeout-era Winter CES
item.description: Commodore draws the Winter CES crowds with two 64K machines, built-in productivity software and a new BASIC—while leaving price and compatibility questions open. The International Winter Consumer Electronics Show opened in Las Vegas on January 7 and ran through January 10; COMPUTE! estimated attendance at 80,000-90,000 and said the Commodore stand was crowded throughout the show. Commodore announced the 264 and speech-equipped 364V, both with 64K RAM and a 7501-family processor running at about 1.76 MHz. Also this week: Behind a secret CES door, Amiga shows 'Lorraine' · Home-computer boom gives way to a fight for survival · Kodak jumps into home video with a one-piece 8mm camcorder.
